     Jain, Kuek, Martin and Stephan, Learners Based on Transducers, Information and Computation (2021): https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~sanjay/paps/transducerlearn.pdf
description: If an automatic family of languages is identifiable in the limit from positive examples by an automatic learner with unrestricted memory, must it also be learnable when its memory length is bounded by the longest example seen, up to an additive constant? The learner must succeed on every text enumerating the target language; equivalent automatic hypothesis codings may be chosen.

author: Sanjay Jain
title: Automatic iterative learning versus hypothesis-sized memory
text:
Does allowing an automatic learner additional memory bounded by the length of its current hypothesis strictly increase what it can identify in the limit from positive data, compared with retaining only the previous hypothesis? Compare learnable automatic families allowing suitable automatic hypothesis-space recodings, rather than fixing a potentially restrictive original indexing.

     Remark: The question concerns positive examples without a counterexample oracle. The 2017 paper already proves iterative learning of automatic families consisting only of infinite languages when bounded negative counterexamples are supplied.

     References:
     Jain, Kinber and Stephan, Automatic Learning from Positive Data and Negative Counterexamples, Information and Computation 255 (2017), introduction: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ic.2017.05.002
description: Does allowing an automatic learner additional memory bounded by the length of its current hypothesis strictly increase what it can identify in the limit from positive data, compared with retaining only the previous hypothesis? Compare learnable automatic families allowing suitable automatic hypothesis-space recodings, rather than fixing a potentially restrictive original indexing.

author: Amit Sahai
title: Witness encryption from plain LWE
text:
Can witness encryption for every NP relation be built from ordinary LWE hardness alone? A satisfying witness must decrypt, while encryptions of different messages must be indistinguishable whenever the public NP statement is false.

     Remark: Editorial continuation of Sahai’s introduction of witness encryption. Evasive-LWE constructions use an additional assumption; this target is weaker than full obfuscation, so solving it need not solve the preceding problem.

     References:
     Garg, Gentry, Sahai and Waters, Witness Encryption and its Applications, STOC (2013): https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258
     Vaikuntanathan, Wee and Wichs, Witness Encryption and Null-IO from Evasive LWE (2022): https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1140
description: Can witness encryption for every NP relation be built from ordinary LWE hardness alone? A satisfying witness must decrypt, while encryptions of different messages must be indistinguishable whenever the public NP statement is false.

author: Mihir Bellare
title: Dual pseudorandom functions from arbitrary one-way functions
text:
Does the existence of any one-way function imply a dual pseudorandom function—one remaining pseudorandom when the roles of its key and input are interchanged? Bellare–Lysyanskaya obtained constructions from one-way permutations or collision-resistant hashing, leaving the minimal-assumption question open.

     References:
     Bellare and Lysyanskaya, Symmetric and Dual PRFs from Standard Assumptions: A Generic Validation of a Prevailing Assumption, Journal of Cryptology (2024): https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-024-09513-6
description: Does the existence of any one-way function imply a dual pseudorandom function—one remaining pseudorandom when the roles of its key and input are interchanged? Bellare–Lysyanskaya obtained constructions from one-way permutations or collision-resistant hashing, leaving the minimal-assumption question open.

author: Dan Boneh
title: General functional encryption from plain LWE
text:
Construct public-key functional encryption for arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, secure against any polynomial number of colluding functional-key holders, from ordinary LWE alone. This is an assumption-focused continuation of Boneh, Sahai and Waters’ general functional-encryption program; bounded-collusion constructions do not meet the target.

     References:
     Boneh, Sahai and Waters, Functional Encryption: Definitions and Challenges, TCC 2011: https://eprint.iacr.org/2010/543.pdf
     Fine-grained polynomial functional encryption, Theoretical Computer Science, 2024 (introduction distinguishes general-circuit and bounded-collusion constructions): https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304397524003475
description: Construct public-key functional encryption for arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, secure against any polynomial number of colluding functional-key holders, from ordinary LWE alone. This is an assumption-focused continuation of Boneh, Sahai and Waters’ general functional-encryption program; bounded-collusion constructions do not meet the target.

author: Yevgeniy Dodis
title: Efficient split-state non-malleable codes approaching capacity
text:
Construct explicit, polynomial-time encodable and decodable, information-theoretic non-malleable codes against arbitrary independent tampering of two shares, with negligible error and rate approaching 1/2. This strengthens the split-state constructions developed by Aggarwal, Dodis and Lovett toward the information-theoretic capacity.

     Remark: Editorial continuation of Dodis’s constructions; the later rate-1/3 result does not attain capacity. Computational-security or additional-state constructions do not settle this information-theoretic two-share target.

     References:
     Aggarwal, Dodis and Lovett, Non-malleable Codes from Additive Combinatorics, STOC 2014: https://cs.nyu.edu/~dodis/ps/nmc.pdf
     Aggarwal, Kanukurthi, Obbattu, Obremski and Sekar, Rate One-Third Non-malleable Codes (2022 revision): https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2021/117/
description: Construct explicit, polynomial-time encodable and decodable, information-theoretic non-malleable codes against arbitrary independent tampering of two shares, with negligible error and rate approaching 1/2. This strengthens the split-state constructions developed by Aggarwal, Dodis and Lovett toward the information-theoretic capacity.

author: Yevgeniy Dodis
title: Verifiable random functions from one-way functions alone
text:
Do one-way functions suffice to construct fully adaptively secure, publicly verifiable random functions on exponentially large input domains in the standard model? This asks whether the extra algebraic assumptions in constructions such as Dodis–Yampolskiy can be eliminated.

     Remark: Editorial foundational extension of his VRF work. Known black-box separations from one-way permutations rule out that approach, rather than settling the unrestricted implication.

     References:
     Dodis and Yampolskiy, A Verifiable Random Function with Short Proofs and Keys, PKC 2005: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-30580-4_28
     Brakerski, Goldwasser, Rothblum and Vaikuntanathan, Weak Verifiable Random Functions, TCC 2009: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-00457-5_33
description: Do one-way functions suffice to construct fully adaptively secure, publicly verifiable random functions on exponentially large input domains in the standard model? This asks whether the extra algebraic assumptions in constructions such as Dodis–Yampolskiy can be eliminated.

author: Stefano Tessaro
title: Compact general-circuit homomorphic secret sharing from DDH
text:
Can the decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption yield two-party, one-private additive homomorphic secret sharing for arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, with output shares whose size is independent of the evaluated circuit? Existing DDH constructions support restricted computations, while general-circuit constructions use stronger tools such as fully homomorphic encryption.

     Remark: Editorial specialization of the paper’s explicit question about general-circuit HSS under assumptions beyond those supporting FHE.

     References:
     Boyle, Gilboa, Ishai, Lin and Tessaro, Foundations of Homomorphic Secret Sharing, ITCS 2018, Section 6: https://sites.cs.ucsb.edu/~tessaro/papers/hss.pdf
description: Can the decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption yield two-party, one-private additive homomorphic secret sharing for arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, with output shares whose size is independent of the evaluated circuit? Existing DDH constructions support restricted computations, while general-circuit constructions use stronger tools such as fully homomorphic encryption.

author: Vipul Goyal
title: Constant-round concurrent zero knowledge from LWE alone
text:
Can LWE alone yield a constant-round zero-knowledge argument for every NP language in the plain model that remains secure under arbitrary polynomially many interleaved sessions, with polynomial-time simulation? This removes the bounded-player restriction from Goyal and coauthors’ constant-round protocols without assuming obfuscation.

     Remark: Editorial minimal-assumption target: unrestricted constant-round concurrent zero knowledge already exists from stronger obfuscation assumptions. Results with superpolynomial-time simulation do not meet the stated requirement.

     References:
     Goyal, Jain, Ostrovsky, Richelson and Visconti, Constant-Round Concurrent Zero Knowledge in the Bounded Player Model, ASIACRYPT 2013: https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~abhishek/papers/bpmodel.pdf
     Canetti, Lin and Pass, Constant-Round Concurrent Zero-Knowledge from Indistinguishability Obfuscation, CRYPTO 2015: https://www.iacr.org/archive/crypto2015/92160262/92160262.pdf
description: Can LWE alone yield a constant-round zero-knowledge argument for every NP language in the plain model that remains secure under arbitrary polynomially many interleaved sessions, with polynomial-time simulation? This removes the bounded-player restriction from Goyal and coauthors’ constant-round protocols without assuming obfuscation.

author: Abhishek Jain
title: Succinct noninteractive arguments for NP from LWE alone
text:
Construct succinct noninteractive arguments for all NP relations in the common-reference-string model from ordinary LWE alone, with proof size poly(λ,log T) and verification time poly(λ,|x|,log T) for T-step witness verification. No random oracle or knowledge assumption is allowed.

     Remark: Editorial extension from deterministic computations to general NP. The June 2026 construction assumes LWE together with SXDH, derandomization and a new proof-complexity assumption, so does not settle the LWE-only target.

     References:
     Choudhuri, Abhishek Jain and Jin, SNARGs for P from LWE, FOCS (2021): https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/808
     Hsieh, Abhishek Jain, Li and Mathialagan, SNARGs for NP from Unprovability of Mathematical Theorems (June 2026): https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/098/
description: Construct succinct noninteractive arguments for all NP relations in the common-reference-string model from ordinary LWE alone, with proof size poly(λ,log T) and verification time poly(λ,|x|,log T) for T-step witness verification. No random oracle or knowledge assumption is allowed.

author: Daniel Wichs
title: Doubly efficient PIR with quasilinear server preprocessing
text:
Can single-server private information retrieval achieve N·polylog N server preprocessing time and storage together with polylog N online query time and communication under standard assumptions such as Ring LWE? The server preprocesses the public N-bit database by itself, and clients retain only poly(λ,log N) state.

     Remark: Editorial tightening of their N^{1+ε} preprocessing/storage guarantee for every fixed ε>0; their polylogarithmic online query complexity is already achieved. Client-specific preprocessing or extra noncolluding servers changes the problem.

     References:
     Lin, Mook and Wichs, Doubly Efficient Private Information Retrieval and Fully Homomorphic RAM Computation from Ring LWE, STOC (2023): https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1703
description: Can single-server private information retrieval achieve N·polylog N server preprocessing time and storage together with polylog N online query time and communication under standard assumptions such as Ring LWE? The server preprocesses the public N-bit database by itself, and clients retain only poly(λ,log N) state.

author: David Chaum
title: Blind signatures from one-way functions alone
text:
Does the existence of one-way functions imply classical blind signatures in the plain model, with blindness and one-more unforgeability against polynomial-time adversaries? Allow arbitrary polynomially many rounds and non-black-box techniques, but no trusted setup or ideal random oracle.

     Remark: Editorial continuation of Chaum’s blind-signature primitive. The 2011 impossibility concerns black-box constructions; the 2026 OWF-based construction uses a global non-programmable random oracle and therefore does not settle the plain-model question.

     References:
     Chaum, Blind Signatures for Untraceable Payments, CRYPTO 1982 proceedings (1983): https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-0602-4_18
     Katz, Schröder and Yerukhimovich, Impossibility of Blind Signatures from One-Way Permutations, TCC 2011: https://www.dominique-schroeder.de/publications/2011_Impossibility_of_Blind_Signatures_from_One-Way_Permutations.pdf
     Ciampi, Della Monica and Visconti, Round-Optimal GUC-Secure Blind Signatures from Minimal Computational and Setup Assumptions, CRYPTO 2026: https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1776515
description: Does the existence of one-way functions imply classical blind signatures in the plain model, with blindness and one-more unforgeability against polynomial-time adversaries? Allow arbitrary polynomially many rounds and non-black-box techniques, but no trusted setup or ideal random oracle.

author: Saharon Shelah
title: Rigidity of the computably enumerable degrees
text:
Is every order automorphism of the partially ordered set of computably enumerable Turing degrees the identity? This asks whether a computably enumerable degree is determined by its position in the reducibility ordering.

     Remark: Editorial continuation of Harrington–Shelah’s structural analysis, not a claim that Shelah personally posed this rigidity conjecture. The structure here is the c.e. degrees, not the full Turing degrees.

     References:
     Harrington and Shelah, The Undecidability of the Recursively Enumerable Degrees, Bulletin AMS (1982): https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-1982-14970-9
     Nies, Shore and Slaman, Definability in the Recursively Enumerable Degrees (1996), structural and rigidity program: https://richardashore.github.io/papers/pdf/bsl10.pdf
description: Is every order automorphism of the partially ordered set of computably enumerable Turing degrees the identity? This asks whether a computably enumerable degree is determined by its position in the reducibility ordering.

author: Saharon Shelah
title: Deciding the two-quantifier theory of c.e. degrees
text:
Is the ∀∃ fragment of the first-order theory of computably enumerable Turing degrees decidable in the language containing only the ordering relation? Harrington–Shelah proved the full theory undecidable, but locating the exact boundary between decidable and undecidable fragments remains open.

     Remark: Editorial continuation of their undecidability theorem. Adding join or meet operations changes the question and can make the two-quantifier fragment undecidable.

     References:
     Harrington and Shelah, The Undecidability of the Recursively Enumerable Degrees, Bulletin AMS (1982): https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-1982-14970-9
     Soskova, One Point Extensions of Antichains, Luminy (2022): https://www.computability.org/luminy2022/abstracts/MariyaSoskova.pdf
description: Is the ∀∃ fragment of the first-order theory of computably enumerable Turing degrees decidable in the language containing only the ordering relation? Harrington–Shelah proved the full theory undecidable, but locating the exact boundary between decidable and undecidable fragments remains open.

author: Julia F. Knight
title: The low_n Boolean algebra conjecture
text:
For every finite n, does any countable Boolean algebra having a low_n presentation also have a computable presentation? Here low_n means that the n-th Turing jump of its atomic diagram is equivalent to the n-th jump of the computable sets; Knight and Stob established the result through n=4.

     References:
     Knight and Stob, Computable Boolean Algebras, Journal of Symbolic Logic (2000): https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-symbolic-logic/article/abs/computable-boolean-algebras/BA70E30949B59AFFEED85E0B62BBC053
     Hirschfeldt, Some Questions in Computable Mathematics (2016), section 1: https://math.uchicago.edu/~drh/Papers/Papers/open.pdf
description: For every finite n, does any countable Boolean algebra having a low_n presentation also have a computable presentation? Here low_n means that the n-th Turing jump of its atomic diagram is equivalent to the n-th jump of the computable sets; Knight and Stob established the result through n=4.

author: Rodney G. Downey
title: The low₂ supersets lattice conjecture
text:
For every coinfinite computably enumerable low₂ set A, is the lattice of its computably enumerable supersets modulo finite difference isomorphic to the entire lattice of computably enumerable sets modulo finite difference? Here low₂ means A″ has the same Turing degree as the double jump of the computable sets.

     Remark: The authors explicitly state that earlier claims of a full proof have not settled the conjecture; their 2025 theorem establishes important special cases involving hyperhypersimple supersets.

     References:
     P. Cholak, R. Downey and N. Greenberg, Low₂ computably enumerable sets have hyperhypersimple supersets, Journal of Symbolic Logic 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01939
description: For every coinfinite computably enumerable low₂ set A, is the lattice of its computably enumerable supersets modulo finite difference isomorphic to the entire lattice of computably enumerable sets modulo finite difference? Here low₂ means A″ has the same Turing degree as the double jump of the computable sets.

author: Richard A. Shore
title: Biinterpretability of computably enumerable degrees with arithmetic
text:
Can standard arithmetic be interpreted inside the pure order of computably enumerable Turing degrees with a definable coding map assigning each degree an index for a c.e. set of that same degree? This would upgrade Nies–Shore–Slaman’s biinterpretability up to the double jump to full recovery of individual c.e. degrees.

     References:
     Nies, Shore and Slaman, Interpretability and Definability in the Recursively Enumerable Degrees, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society 77 (1998), introduction. https://richardashore.github.io/papers/pdf/def8o.pdf
description: Can standard arithmetic be interpreted inside the pure order of computably enumerable Turing degrees with a definable coding map assigning each degree an index for a c.e. set of that same degree? This would upgrade Nies–Shore–Slaman’s biinterpretability up to the double jump to full recovery of individual c.e. degrees.

author: Steffen Lempp
title: Deciding finite-lattice embeddability into c.e. degrees
text:
Is there an algorithm deciding which finite lattices embed into the computably enumerable Turing degrees while preserving joins and meets? A structural characterization would explain which finite patterns of relative computability can occur.

     References:
     Lempp, Lerman and Solomon, Embedding Finite Lattices into the Computably Enumerable Degrees—A Status Survey, Logic Colloquium 2002 (published 2006): https://people.math.wisc.edu/~slempp/papers/muenster.pdf
description: Is there an algorithm deciding which finite lattices embed into the computably enumerable Turing degrees while preserving joins and meets? A structural characterization would explain which finite patterns of relative computability can occur.

author: Steffen Lempp
title: The two-quantifier theory of the local enumeration degrees
text:
Is the ∀∃ first-order theory of the Σ⁰₂ enumeration degrees decidable, in the language of their partial order? Lempp and collaborators’ work on Ahmad pairs resolves specific configurations needed for such a decision procedure but leaves the general theory.

     References:
     Kalimullin, Lempp, Ng and Yamaleev, On Cupping and Ahmad Pairs, JSL (2024): https://people.math.wisc.edu/~slempp/papers/nocup.pdf
description: Is the ∀∃ first-order theory of the Σ⁰₂ enumeration degrees decidable, in the language of their partial order? Lempp and collaborators’ work on Ahmad pairs resolves specific configurations needed for such a decision procedure but leaves the general theory.

author: Philip D. Welch
title: Classifying sets with countable infinite-time decision complexity
text:
Characterize, in terms of the constructible hierarchy, the sets of reals decidable by an infinite-time Turing machine with a countable uniform bound on its halting times, and the corresponding semidecidable classes. The known suprema of possible times do not characterize which sets have such algorithms.

     References:
     Carl, Schlicht and Welch, Decision Times of Infinite Computations, Notre Dame J. Formal Logic (2022), Question 6.1: https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.04942
description: Characterize, in terms of the constructible hierarchy, the sets of reals decidable by an infinite-time Turing machine with a countable uniform bound on its halting times, and the corresponding semidecidable classes. The known suprema of possible times do not characterize which sets have such algorithms.

author: Philip D. Welch
title: Admissibility of gaps in infinite-time decision times
text:
Must every ordinal beginning a gap in the attainable countable decision times, or in the attainable countable semidecision times, be admissible? Here a set’s time is the least uniform supremum of halting times among its infinite-time algorithms.

     Remark: The analogous theorem for clockable ordinals does not settle these decision-time spectra.

     References:
     Carl, Schlicht and Welch, Decision Times of Infinite Computations (2022), Question 6.3: https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.04942
description: Must every ordinal beginning a gap in the attainable countable decision times, or in the attainable countable semidecision times, be admissible? Here a set’s time is the least uniform supremum of halting times among its infinite-time algorithms.

author: Greg Hjorth
title: Universality of recursive isomorphism on binary sequences
text:
Is every countable Borel equivalence relation Borel reducible to recursive isomorphism on 2^omega, where two binary sequences are equivalent when a computable permutation of their coordinates transforms one into the other?

     Remark: Editorial continuation of Hjorth’s joint universality results: universality on five-symbol sequences, and subsequently three-symbol sequences, is established; the binary case and its merely measure-universal version must be distinguished.

     References:
     Andretta, Camerlo and Hjorth, Conjugacy equivalence relation on subgroups, Fundamenta Mathematicae 167 (2001), 189–212; discussed in Marks, §§1 and 3.5: https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/papers/uurt_v5.pdf
description: Is every countable Borel equivalence relation Borel reducible to recursive isomorphism on 2^omega, where two binary sequences are equivalent when a computable permutation of their coordinates transforms one into the other?

author: Keng Meng Ng
title: An infinite topologically computably categorical Polish space
text:
Does there exist an infinite computable Polish space for which every two computable presentations are related by a computable homeomorphism? This asks whether any infinite complete separable space can have fully effective topological uniqueness.

     References:
     Ng, §8, Problems 27–28, in Barmpalias et al., Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory (2025): https://arxiv.org/html/2507.03972v1#S8
description: Does there exist an infinite computable Polish space for which every two computable presentations are related by a computable homeomorphism? This asks whether any infinite complete separable space can have fully effective topological uniqueness.

author: Keng Meng Ng
title: The degree of topological categoricity of Baire space
text:
Is there a least Turing degree d such that every two computable presentations of Baire space omega^omega admit a d-computable homeomorphism? If such a degree exists, identify it.

     Remark: The maps are homeomorphisms rather than isometries; this is the topological categoricity problem stated by Ng, not ordinary categoricity of a discrete structure.

     References:
     Ng, §8, Problems 27–28, in Barmpalias et al., Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory (2025): https://arxiv.org/html/2507.03972v1#S8
description: Is there a least Turing degree d such that every two computable presentations of Baire space omega^omega admit a d-computable homeomorphism? If such a degree exists, identify it.

author: Leah Epstein
title: The optimal competitive ratio of online bin packing
text:
Determine the smallest asymptotic competitive ratio for deterministic online bin packing, with each arriving item irrevocably placed in a unit-capacity bin. The gap between the approximately 1.54278 lower bound and 1.57829 upper bound remains the central target of this research line.

     References:
     Balogh, Békési, Dósa, Epstein and Levin, A New Lower Bound for Classic Online Bin Packing (2018): https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05554
description: Determine the smallest asymptotic competitive ratio for deterministic online bin packing, with each arriving item irrevocably placed in a unit-capacity bin. The gap between the approximately 1.54278 lower bound and 1.57829 upper bound remains the central target of this research line.

author: Jirí Sgall
title: The optimal stretch for online bin stretching
text:
Determine the smallest worst-case stretch achievable by deterministic online packing into m bins when the entire item sequence is promised to fit offline in m unit bins. Items must be assigned irrevocably, and the central target is the optimal ratio for arbitrarily large m.

     Remark: The 3/2 barrier was already broken before the cutoff: the cited paper gives 139/93<1.495 for sufficiently large m. The remaining question is the optimal ratio.

     References:
     M. Böhm, M. Lieskovský, S. Schmitt, J. Sgall and R. van Stee, Improved online load balancing with known makespan, APPROX/RANDOM 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08376
description: Determine the smallest worst-case stretch achievable by deterministic online packing into m bins when the entire item sequence is promised to fit offline in m unit bins. Items must be assigned irrevocably, and the central target is the optimal ratio for arbitrarily large m.

author: Thomas Erlebach
title: The optimal deterministic price of obligatory testing
text:
What is the optimal deterministic competitive ratio for minimizing total completion time on one machine when all jobs are initially present, each requires a known-duration test, and its processing time is revealed only by that test? Tests and processing operations are individually nonpreemptive; the general-test-time gap is between √2 and 1.861.

     References:
     Dogeas, Erlebach and Liang, Scheduling with Obligatory Tests, ESA 2024, Section 5: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16734
description: What is the optimal deterministic competitive ratio for minimizing total completion time on one machine when all jobs are initially present, each requires a known-duration test, and its processing time is revealed only by that test? Tests and processing operations are individually nonpreemptive; the general-test-time gap is between √2 and 1.861.

author: Thomas Erlebach
title: The power of randomization in scheduling with obligatory tests
text:
Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary for single-machine total completion time when every initially available job must undergo a unit-time test revealing its unknown processing time. Both test and processing operations are nonpreemptive, and the offline optimum must also test every job.

     Remark: This is the randomized direction explicitly proposed in the paper; the deterministic uniform-test bounds are √2 and 1.585. The 2026 result on gradually arriving jobs concerns flow time and does not resolve this all-jobs-present model: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12716

     References:
     Dogeas, Erlebach and Liang, Scheduling with Obligatory Tests, ESA 2024, Section 5: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16734
description: Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary for single-machine total completion time when every initially available job must undergo a unit-time test revealing its unknown processing time. Both test and processing operations are nonpreemptive, and the offline optimum must also test every job.

author: Marcin Bienkowski
title: Optimal deterministic competitive ratio for file migration
text:
Is there a 3-competitive deterministic algorithm for file migration on arbitrary metric spaces, where serving a request costs its distance from the file and moving the file costs D times the distance moved? Bienkowski–Byrka–Mucha achieve ratio 4, while the general lower bound is 3.

     References:
     M. Bienkowski, J. Byrka and M. Mucha, Dynamic Beats Fixed: On Phase-Based Algorithms for File Migration, ICALP 2017: https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2017.13
description: Is there a 3-competitive deterministic algorithm for file migration on arbitrary metric spaces, where serving a request costs its distance from the file and moving the file costs D times the distance moved? Bienkowski–Byrka–Mucha achieve ratio 4, while the general lower bound is 3.

author: Kirk Pruhs
title: Polynomial-time constant approximation for the General Scheduling Problem
text:
For preemptive scheduling on one machine, with release times and arbitrary nonnegative nondecreasing job-specific completion-cost functions, is there a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to the sum of costs? This asks to improve the O(log log P) guarantee of Bansal and Pruhs, where P is the ratio of largest to smallest processing time.

     Remark: The November 2025 constant-factor result is quasipolynomial-time and assumes quasipolynomially bounded integer processing times; it does not resolve the polynomial-time question.

     References:
     N. Bansal and K. Pruhs, The Geometry of Scheduling, SICOMP 2014: https://doi.org/10.1137/130911317
     A. Armbruster, L. Rohwedder and A. Wiese, A (2+epsilon)-approximation algorithm for the general scheduling problem in quasipolynomial time, November 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16536
description: For preemptive scheduling on one machine, with release times and arbitrary nonnegative nondecreasing job-specific completion-cost functions, is there a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to the sum of costs? This asks to improve the O(log log P) guarantee of Bansal and Pruhs, where P is the ratio of largest to smallest processing time.

author: Tjark Vredeveld
title: The optimal prophet-secretary constant
text:
What is the largest universal α such that, for independent nonnegative values drawn from known distributions and revealed in uniformly random order, an online algorithm selecting at most one value guarantees α times the expected maximum? Closing this optimal-stopping gap continues the random-arrival problem studied in Vredeveld and coauthors’ work and survey.

     References:
     J. Correa, P. Foncea, R. Hoeksma, T. Oosterwijk and T. Vredeveld, Recent Developments in Prophet Inequalities, SIGecom Exchanges 17(1), 61–70 (2018/2019): https://www.dii.uchile.cl/~jcorrea/papers/Journals/CFHOV2019.pdf
     Z. Chen, Z. Huang, D. Li and Z. G. Tang, Prophet Secretary and Matching: the Significance of the Largest Item, SODA 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.01191
description: What is the largest universal α such that, for independent nonnegative values drawn from known distributions and revealed in uniformly random order, an online algorithm selecting at most one value guarantees α times the expected maximum? Closing this optimal-stopping gap continues the random-arrival problem studied in Vredeveld and coauthors’ work and survey.

source_id: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times/1B
area: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
author: Uriel Feige
title: The exact minimum stationary-start cover time
text:
Does every irreducible discrete-time reversible Markov chain on n states satisfy Eπ[C]≥(n−1)H_{n−1}, where the walk starts in stationarity and C is the time to visit all states? This exact bound would strengthen the extremal cover-time line in which Feige established the asymptotic n log n lower bound for unweighted graphs.

     Remark: Editorial extension of Feige’s extremal cover-time work; the exact reversible-chain conjecture is stated by Aldous and Fill.

     References:
     Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, Open Problem 6.30 and discussion of Feige’s theorem: https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/Book_Ralph/Ch6.S6.html
description: Does every irreducible discrete-time reversible Markov chain on n states satisfy Eπ[C]≥(n−1)H_{n−1}, where the walk starts in stationarity and C is the time to visit all states? This exact bound would strengthen the extremal cover-time line in which Feige established the asymptotic n log n lower bound for unweighted graphs.

source_id: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times/5A
area: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
author: Jennifer Tour Chayes
title: Polynomial mixing at the four-state Potts critical point
text:
Does Swendsen–Wang dynamics for the zero-field ferromagnetic four-state Potts model on an L×L square torus at its critical temperature mix in L^O(1) full cluster updates? This is the remaining four-state case of the predicted polynomial critical slowdown, beyond the known quasipolynomial bound.

     Remark: This is an editorial continuation of Chayes’s work on critical Potts dynamics; polynomial bounds for two and three states do not settle four states.

     References:
     C. Borgs, J. T. Chayes and P. Tetali, Tight Bounds for Mixing of the Swendsen–Wang Algorithm at the Potts Transition Point, Probability Theory and Related Fields 2012: https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.3058
     R. Gheissari and E. Lubetzky, Mixing Times of Critical Two-Dimensional Potts Models, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 2018: https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.02182
description: Does Swendsen–Wang dynamics for the zero-field ferromagnetic four-state Potts model on an L×L square torus at its critical temperature mix in L^O(1) full cluster updates? This is the remaining four-state case of the predicted polynomial critical slowdown, beyond the known quasipolynomial bound.

source_id: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times/5B
area: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
author: Jennifer Tour Chayes
title: The critical dynamic exponent of Swendsen–Wang for the planar Ising model
text:
For the zero-field critical Ising model on an L×L square torus, determine the asymptotic inverse spectral gap of Swendsen–Wang dynamics, in particular whether it is L^(z+o(1)) and the value of z. Count one simultaneous cluster update as one step; a polynomial upper bound alone does not identify the exponent.

     Remark: This is a sharper editorial target within the critical dynamics studied by Chayes and collaborators. Numerical exponent estimates are not rigorous determinations of the spectral-gap asymptotics.

     References:
     C. Borgs, J. T. Chayes and P. Tetali, Tight Bounds for Mixing of the Swendsen–Wang Algorithm at the Potts Transition Point, Probability Theory and Related Fields 2012: https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.3058
     C.-W. Liu, A. Polkovnikov and A. W. Sandvik, Dynamic Scaling at Classical Phase Transitions Approached through Nonequilibrium Quenching, Physical Review B 2014: https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.6327
     R. Gheissari and E. Lubetzky, Mixing Times of Critical Two-Dimensional Potts Models: https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.02182
description: For the zero-field critical Ising model on an L×L square torus, determine the asymptotic inverse spectral gap of Swendsen–Wang dynamics, in particular whether it is L^(z+o(1)) and the value of z. Count one simultaneous cluster update as one step; a polynomial upper bound alone does not identify the exponent.

source_id: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times/7A
area: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
author: Roman Kotecký
title: Cluster sampling of graph colourings at Δ+1 colours
text:
Does Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký dynamics mix in polynomial time on every n-vertex graph of maximum degree Δ when q≥Δ+1 colours are available? A step chooses two colours uniformly and independently swaps them on each connected component induced by those colours, with probability 1/2.

     Remark: This is an editorial sharp-threshold target for Kotecký’s cluster sampler, not a personal conjecture attributed to him. A July 2026 preprint obtains optimal mixing on chordal and outerplanar graphs, without resolving arbitrary graphs.

     References:
     Wang, Swendsen and Kotecký, Antiferromagnetic Potts models, Physical Review Letters 63 (1989): https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.63.109
     Wang, Yoshida and Zhang, Approximate Colorwise Tensorization of Entropy and Optimal Mixing of the Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký Dynamics (July 2026), introduction and Section 6: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10119
description: Does Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký dynamics mix in polynomial time on every n-vertex graph of maximum degree Δ when q≥Δ+1 colours are available? A step chooses two colours uniformly and independently swaps them on each connected component induced by those colours, with probability 1/2.

source_id: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times/7B
area: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
author: Roman Kotecký
title: Rapid cluster sampling of three-colourings on the square torus
text:
Prove a polynomial upper bound on the worst-case total-variation mixing time of Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký dynamics for uniform proper three-colourings of an N×N square torus, with N even. This would rigorously explain the sampler’s effectiveness at the critical antiferromagnetic point.

     Remark: The July 2026 paper still lists obtaining a mixing upper bound on this torus as open; numerical observations of very fast relaxation are not a mixing-time proof.

     References:
     Wang, Swendsen and Kotecký, Three-state antiferromagnetic Potts models: A Monte Carlo study, Physical Review B 42 (1990): https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.42.2465
     Wang, Yoshida and Zhang, Approximate Colorwise Tensorization of Entropy and Optimal Mixing of the Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký Dynamics (July 2026), introduction and Section 6: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10119
description: Prove a polynomial upper bound on the worst-case total-variation mixing time of Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký dynamics for uniform proper three-colourings of an N×N square torus, with N even. This would rigorously explain the sampler’s effectiveness at the critical antiferromagnetic point.

source_id: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times/11A
area: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
author: Dana Randall
title: The hard-core transition on the square lattice
text:
Establish and locate a sharp critical activity separating uniqueness from phase coexistence in the hard-core model on Z², where independent sets have weight proportional to λ raised to their size. Closing the gap between rigorous uniqueness and coexistence regimes would clarify the transition underlying Randall’s sampling and mixing-time results.

     References:
     Blanca, Chen, Galvin, Randall and Tetali, Phase Coexistence for the Hard-Core Model on Z² (2019): https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01115
description: Establish and locate a sharp critical activity separating uniqueness from phase coexistence in the hard-core model on Z², where independent sets have weight proportional to λ raised to their size. Closing the gap between rigorous uniqueness and coexistence regimes would clarify the transition underlying Randall’s sampling and mixing-time results.

author: Arturo Merino
title: Ranking and unranking a spanning-tree Gray code
text:
Find an ordering of all spanning trees of the complete graph K_n in which successive trees exchange one edge and both ranking a tree and recovering the tree of a given rank take polynomial time in n. Such an ordering would combine minimal-change enumeration with efficient random access.

     References:
     Merino and Mütze, Traversing Combinatorial 0/1-Polytopes via Optimization, §9, SICOMP 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08567
description: Find an ordering of all spanning trees of the complete graph K_n in which successive trees exchange one edge and both ranking a tree and recovering the tree of a given rank take polynomial time in n. Such an ordering would combine minimal-change enumeration with efficient random access.

author: Torsten Mütze
title: Pivot-exchange Gray codes for spanning trees
text:
Does every connected undirected graph admit a listing of all its spanning trees exactly once in which each transition deletes and inserts edges sharing an endpoint? The known construction for outerplanar triangulations leaves the unrestricted graph case open.

     References:
     Behrooznia and Mütze, Listing Spanning Trees of Outerplanar Graphs by Pivot-Exchanges, STACS 2025, Problem 1: https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.STACS.2025.16
description: Does every connected undirected graph admit a listing of all its spanning trees exactly once in which each transition deletes and inserts edges sharing an endpoint? The known construction for outerplanar triangulations leaves the unrestricted graph case open.

author: Torsten Mütze
title: Edge-exchange Gray codes for directed spanning trees
text:
For every directed graph and fixed root, can all spanning arborescences directed away from that root be listed so that successive arborescences exchange exactly one arc? This is Knuth’s directed spanning-tree Gray-code problem, presented alongside the authors’ undirected results.

     Remark: The directed question is stronger than the preceding undirected question; they are distinct models of the same enumeration programme.

     References:
     Behrooznia and Mütze, Listing Spanning Trees of Outerplanar Graphs by Pivot-Exchanges, STACS 2025, Problem 2: https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.STACS.2025.16
description: For every directed graph and fixed root, can all spanning arborescences directed away from that root be listed so that successive arborescences exchange exactly one arc? This is Knuth’s directed spanning-tree Gray-code problem, presented alongside the authors’ undirected results.

author: Namrata
title: Polynomial-delay disjointness Gray codes for combinations
text:
For n≥2k+1, excluding (n,k)=(5,2), generate a cyclic ordering of all k-subsets of [n] in which consecutive sets are disjoint, using polynomial(n,k) time per generated set. The existence of such an ordering is proved, but the construction is not yet efficient in these parameters.

     Remark: Namrata is the researcher publishing under that single name, as confirmed by her publication page: https://sites.google.com/view/nnamrata/publications . The Kneser Hamiltonicity existence conjecture itself is already solved.

     References:
     Merino, Mütze and Namrata, Kneser graphs are Hamiltonian, STOC 2023 / full version February 2025, §1.5 and conclusion: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.03918
description: For n≥2k+1, excluding (n,k)=(5,2), generate a cyclic ordering of all k-subsets of [n] in which consecutive sets are disjoint, using polynomial(n,k) time per generated set. The existence of such an ordering is proved, but the construction is not yet efficient in these parameters.

author: Peter Sanders
title: Rank error of MultiQueues under unrestricted insertion orders
text:
For the basic MultiQueue with q internal priority queues, uniformly random insertions, and deletion of the smaller minimum from two random queues, determine the worst-case expected rank error over oblivious operation and key sequences. In particular, does an O(q) bound survive when insertions can introduce keys smaller than previously deleted keys?

     References:
     Williams and Sanders, Engineering MultiQueues: Fast Relaxed Concurrent Priority Queues, 2025, analysis and outlook: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11652
description: For the basic MultiQueue with q internal priority queues, uniformly random insertions, and deletion of the smaller minimum from two random queues, determine the worst-case expected rank error over oblivious operation and key sequences. In particular, does an O(q) bound survive when insertions can introduce keys smaller than previously deleted keys?

author: Peter Sanders
title: Fast insertion arbitrarily close to bucketized-cuckoo thresholds
text:
For two-choice cuckoo hashing with bucket capacity b, obtain insertion time bounded independently of table size throughout the feasible load range below its sharp orientability threshold, with explicit dependence on the distance to that threshold. This is an editorial theoretical extension of Sanders’s space-efficient bucketized hash-table work.

     Remark: Later progress: Bell and Kuszmaul’s July 2026 preprint gives an insertion procedure with table-size-independent expected time for loads 1−(1+δ)ε*, where ε* is the threshold slack and δ≥0.99^b, and O(1) amortized expected evictions. This covers a substantial near-threshold range; it is not a claim that every remaining parameter regime or the traditional random-walk rule is settled.

     References:
     Maier and Sanders, Dynamic Space Efficient Hashing, ESA 2017: https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.00997
     Bell and Kuszmaul, Fast Insertion for Bucketized Cuckoo Hashing, July 2026: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24545
description: For two-choice cuckoo hashing with bucket capacity b, obtain insertion time bounded independently of table size throughout the feasible load range below its sharp orientability threshold, with explicit dependence on the distance to that threshold. This is an editorial theoretical extension of Sanders’s space-efficient bucketized hash-table work.

author: Fedor V. Fomin
title: Polylogarithmic updates for bounded rank-width
text:
Can a graph that always has rank-width at most k be maintained under edge insertions and deletions with an implicit rank-decomposition of width O(k) and f(k)polylog(n) amortized update time? This is an editorial data-structure extension of Fomin and Korhonen’s branch-decomposition refinement framework.

     Remark: The dynamic follow-up gives subpolynomial, rather than polylogarithmic, update time. The polylogarithmic dynamic tree-width results concern a different graph parameter.

     References:
     Fomin and Korhonen, Fast FPT-Approximation of Branchwidth, STOC 2022 / SICOMP 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.03492
     Korhonen and Sokołowski, Almost-linear time parameterized algorithm for rankwidth via dynamic rankwidth, 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12364
description: Can a graph that always has rank-width at most k be maintained under edge insertions and deletions with an implicit rank-decomposition of width O(k) and f(k)polylog(n) amortized update time? This is an editorial data-structure extension of Fomin and Korhonen’s branch-decomposition refinement framework.

author: Kurt Mehlhorn
title: The traversal conjecture for splay trees
text:
Starting from any n-key BST, does splaying the keys in the preorder sequence of any other BST on the same keys take O(n) total time? Mehlhorn and coauthors study this fundamental special case through pattern avoidance and obtain relaxations for Greedy.

     Remark: The statement is specifically about Splay; linear-time results for variants of Greedy with preprocessing do not prove it.

     References:
     P. Chalermsook, M. Goswami, L. Kozma, K. Mehlhorn and T. Saranurak, Pattern-Avoiding Access in Binary Search Trees, FOCS 2015: https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.06953
description: Starting from any n-key BST, does splaying the keys in the preorder sequence of any other BST on the same keys take O(n) total time? Mehlhorn and coauthors study this fundamental special case through pattern avoidance and obtain relaxations for Greedy.

author: Michal Pilipczuk
title: Worst-case dynamic Courcelle theorem at bounded treewidth
text:
Under edge insertions and deletions preserving treewidth at most k, can every fixed CMSO₂ graph property be maintained in f(k,φ)·polylog(n) worst-case update time? This is an editorial strengthening of Pilipczuk and coauthors’ dynamic decomposition and logical-property data structures.

     Remark: The amortized polylogarithmic target was already resolved in 2025; the question specifically asks for a worst-case bound.

     References:
     Korhonen, Majewski, Nadara, Pilipczuk and Sokołowski, Dynamic treewidth, FOCS 2023: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01744
     Korhonen, Dynamic Treewidth in Logarithmic Time, FOCS 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02790v2
description: Under edge insertions and deletions preserving treewidth at most k, can every fixed CMSO₂ graph property be maintained in f(k,φ)·polylog(n) worst-case update time? This is an editorial strengthening of Pilipczuk and coauthors’ dynamic decomposition and logical-property data structures.

author: Eva Rotenberg
title: Worst-case polylogarithmic fully dynamic planarity testing
text:
Can a deterministic data structure test planarity after arbitrary edge insertions and deletions in polylogarithmic worst-case time per operation? Holm and Rotenberg achieve polylogarithmic amortized time; the goal is to remove occasional expensive updates.

     References:
     Holm and Rotenberg, Fully-dynamic Planarity Testing in Polylogarithmic Time, STOC 2020: https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03449
description: Can a deterministic data structure test planarity after arbitrary edge insertions and deletions in polylogarithmic worst-case time per operation? Holm and Rotenberg achieve polylogarithmic amortized time; the goal is to remove occasional expensive updates.

author: Saket Saurabh
title: Polylogarithmic updates for the exact arboricity value
text:
Can the exact arboricity of a fully dynamic undirected graph—the minimum number of forests covering its edges—be maintained with polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant-time value queries? This is an editorial target extending Saurabh and coauthors’ exact-maintenance work; it asks only for the value, not explicit maintenance of an optimal forest decomposition.

     Remark: Known near-optimal approximation structures do not give the exact value. Lower bounds for explicitly changing an optimal forest decomposition do not by themselves rule out the value-only target.

     References:
     Banerjee, Raman and Saurabh, Fully dynamic arboricity maintenance, TCS 822 (2020): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tcs.2020.04.010
     de Vos and Christiansen, Tree-Packing Revisited: Faster Fully Dynamic Min-Cut and Arboricity, SODA 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09141v2
description: Can the exact arboricity of a fully dynamic undirected graph—the minimum number of forests covering its edges—be maintained with polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant-time value queries? This is an editorial target extending Saurabh and coauthors’ exact-maintenance work; it asks only for the value, not explicit maintenance of an optimal forest decomposition.

author: Ulrich Meyer
title: Sorting-bound external-memory breadth-first search
text:
Can exact breadth-first distances in an arbitrary undirected graph with n vertices and m edges be computed in O(Sort(n+m)) I/Os, even when its vertex set does not fit in RAM? Here Sort(N)=Θ((N/B)·max{1,log_(M/B)(N/B)}) is the external sorting bound, with memory M and block size B in the standard indivisible-record I/O model.

     Remark: Classification note: this is a foundational external-memory graph-storage and access problem; specialized graph classes and semi-external algorithms do not settle the unrestricted case.

     References:
     K. Mehlhorn and U. Meyer, External-Memory Breadth-First Search with Sublinear I/O, ESA 2002: https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/ftp/ExternalBFS.pdf
description: Can exact breadth-first distances in an arbitrary undirected graph with n vertices and m edges be computed in O(Sort(n+m)) I/Os, even when its vertex set does not fit in RAM? Here Sort(N)=Θ((N/B)·max{1,log_(M/B)(N/B)}) is the external sorting bound, with memory M and block size B in the standard indivisible-record I/O model.

author: Ulrich Meyer
title: Sorting-bound external-memory weighted shortest paths
text:
Can exact single-source shortest paths in an arbitrary undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights be computed using O(Sort(n+m)) I/Os in the same external-memory model? The target allows neither a bounded edge-weight ratio nor an assumption that all vertex records fit in RAM.

     Remark: Editorial sorting-bound target continuing Meyer’s external-memory shortest-path data structures and algorithms.

     References:
     U. Meyer and N. Zeh, I/O-Efficient Undirected Shortest Paths with Unbounded Edge Lengths, ESA 2006: https://doi.org/10.1007/11841036_49
     G. S. Brodal, R. Fagerberg, U. Meyer and N. Zeh, Cache-Oblivious Data Structures and Algorithms for Undirected Breadth-First Search and Shortest Paths, SWAT 2004: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-27810-8_41
description: Can exact single-source shortest paths in an arbitrary undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights be computed using O(Sort(n+m)) I/Os in the same external-memory model? The target allows neither a bounded edge-weight ratio nor an assumption that all vertex records fit in RAM.

author: Dániel Marx
title: Faster approximate dynamic distances on monotone grids
text:
For a directed N-vertex grid with east, north and northeast arcs and nonnegative weights, can fixed opposite-corner distances be maintained within 1+ε with polylog(N)·poly(1/ε) update time and √N polylog(N)·poly(1/ε) query time? Allow polynomial preprocessing and an offline-known sequence of arbitrary weight changes.

     Remark: Editorial benchmark sharpening the paper’s explicit dynamic-grid question; its reduction would yield near-quadratic approximate DTW under translation. Approximation is essential here: exact dynamic planar-distance tradeoffs face conditional lower bounds.

     References:
     K. Bringmann, S. Kisfaludi-Bak, M. Künnemann, D. Marx and A. Nusser, Dynamic Time Warping Under Translation: Approximation Guided by Space-Filling Curves, SoCG 2022 / Journal of Computational Geometry 2023, Section 4: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07898
description: For a directed N-vertex grid with east, north and northeast arcs and nonnegative weights, can fixed opposite-corner distances be maintained within 1+ε with polylog(N)·poly(1/ε) update time and √N polylog(N)·poly(1/ε) query time? Allow polynomial preprocessing and an offline-known sequence of arbitrary weight changes.

author: Marc J. van Kreveld
title: Fully dynamic linear programming with outliers
text:
Can a set of planar halfplane constraints support arbitrary insertions and deletions while maintaining a point minimizing a fixed linear objective and violating at most k constraints, in k^O(1)polylog(n) amortized update time and near-linear-plus-poly(k) space? The deletion time of a constraint must not have to be announced when it is inserted.

     Remark: The cited semi-online structure assumes advance knowledge of deletion times; the fully dynamic extension is an explicit open direction, with the displayed bound an editorial benchmark.

     References:
     E. Glazenburg, M. van Kreveld and F. Staals, Robust Classification of Dynamic Bichromatic Point Sets in R², 2024, open problems following Theorem 5: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19161
description: Can a set of planar halfplane constraints support arbitrary insertions and deletions while maintaining a point minimizing a fixed linear objective and violating at most k constraints, in k^O(1)polylog(n) amortized update time and near-linear-plus-poly(k) space? The deletion time of a constraint must not have to be announced when it is inserted.

author: Fabrizio Grandoni
title: Fast dynamic vertex colouring against adaptive updates
text:
Can a randomized data structure maintain a proper (Δ+1)-vertex colouring in polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an adaptive adversary? The graph undergoes edge insertions and deletions, always has maximum degree at most the known bound Δ, and vertex-colour queries should take constant time.

     Remark: Editorial adversarial-robustness extension: the constant-update result assumes oblivious updates; adaptive-adversary algorithms still had polynomial update bounds at the cutoff.

     References:
     S. Bhattacharya, F. Grandoni, J. Kulkarni, Q. C. Liu and S. Solomon, Fully Dynamic (Δ+1)-Coloring in O(1) Update Time, TALG 2022: https://doi.org/10.1145/3494539
     M. Flin and M. M. Halldórsson, Faster Dynamic (Δ+1)-Coloring Against Adaptive Adversaries, ICALP 2025: https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.79
description: Can a randomized data structure maintain a proper (Δ+1)-vertex colouring in polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an adaptive adversary? The graph undergoes edge insertions and deletions, always has maximum degree at most the known bound Δ, and vertex-colour queries should take constant time.

author: Paolo Ferragina
title: Optimal-query fully dynamic text indexing
text:
Can a length-n text over a fixed alphabet be maintained in O(n) machine words with polylogarithmic amortized time per single-character insertion or deletion and O(m+occ) worst-case time to report all occurrences of a queried length-m pattern? Edits may occur at arbitrary positions, and the word size is Θ(log n).

     Remark: Editorial strengthening of Ferragina and Grossi’s dynamic-indexing problem. Ephemeral edits that are immediately undone and append-only texts are weaker models.

     References:
     P. Ferragina and R. Grossi, Optimal On-Line Search and Sublinear Time Update in String Matching, SIAM Journal on Computing 27 (1998): https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539795286119
     S. P. Pissis, Text Indexing and Pattern Matching with Ephemeral Edits, 2025, related work on fully dynamic indexing: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05124
description: Can a length-n text over a fixed alphabet be maintained in O(n) machine words with polylogarithmic amortized time per single-character insertion or deletion and O(m+occ) worst-case time to report all occurrences of a queried length-m pattern? Edits may occur at arbitrary positions, and the word size is Θ(log n).

author: Gerth Stølting Brodal
title: Logarithmic dynamic convex-hull line intersection queries
text:
Can arbitrary planar-point insertions and deletions and queries for the two intersections of a line with their convex hull all be supported in O(log n) time using linear space? Amortized update time is permitted, but line-intersection queries should take worst-case logarithmic time.

     Remark: This remaining line-stabbing variant is not covered by the optimal bounds for extreme-point and tangent queries.

     References:
     G. S. Brodal and R. Jacob, Dynamic Planar Convex Hull, FOCS 2002: https://cs.au.dk/~gerth/papers/focs02.pdf
     The Open Problems Project, Problem 12, Dynamic Planar Convex Hull (remaining variants): https://topp.openproblem.net/p12
description: Can arbitrary planar-point insertions and deletions and queries for the two intersections of a line with their convex hull all be supported in O(log n) time using linear space? Amortized update time is permitted, but line-intersection queries should take worst-case logarithmic time.

source_id: Game theory, social choice and fair division/9B
area: Game theory, social choice and fair division
author: Jason D. Hartline
title: Optimal truthful pricing from one sample
text:
What is the exact best worst-case revenue ratio obtainable by a randomized posted price computed from one independent sample of an unknown monotone-hazard-rate distribution? The benchmark is the monopoly revenue knowing the distribution; this isolates the truthful side of Hartline’s revelation-gap research.

     Remark: Hartline’s October 2026 survey still gives a gap, placing the optimum between 0.644 and 0.648. Non-truthful mechanisms are a different comparison class.

     References:
     Y. Feng, J. D. Hartline and Y. Li, Revelation Gap for Pricing from Samples, STOC 2021: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.13496
     J. Hartline, Robustness in Mechanism Design, October 2026, section 6.4: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01805
description: What is the exact best worst-case revenue ratio obtainable by a randomized posted price computed from one independent sample of an unknown monotone-hazard-rate distribution? The benchmark is the monopoly revenue knowing the distribution; this isolates the truthful side of Hartline’s revelation-gap research.

source_id: Game theory, social choice and fair division/11A
area: Game theory, social choice and fair division
author: S. Matthew Weinberg
title: Constant-factor welfare from posted item prices
text:
For independent buyers with subadditive valuations over m items, do fixed anonymous item prices chosen from the known value distributions guarantee a universal constant fraction of expected optimal welfare, regardless of arrival order? This asks for posted prices specifically, beyond the known O(log log m) approximation.

     Remark: Constant-factor combinatorial prophet inequalities using more general allocation rules do not settle this posted-price question.

     References:
     K. Bangachev and S. M. Weinberg, Improved Welfare Guarantees for Posted-Price Mechanisms, ICALP 2025: https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.18
     K. Bangachev and S. M. Weinberg, 2023 preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01451
description: For independent buyers with subadditive valuations over m items, do fixed anonymous item prices chosen from the known value distributions guarantee a universal constant fraction of expected optimal welfare, regardless of arrival order? This asks for posted prices specifically, beyond the known O(log log m) approximation.

source_id: Game theory, social choice and fair division/13A
area: Game theory, social choice and fair division
author: Moshe Tennenholtz
title: Optimal randomized truthful two-facility location
text:
What is the smallest worst-case expected social-cost approximation ratio achievable by a truthful-in-expectation mechanism placing two facilities on the real line without payments? Agents privately report their locations, each incurs distance to the nearer facility, and social cost is the sum of these distances.

     Remark: Editorial sharp-ratio target in their foundational model. The 2026 preprint improves the upper bound from 4 to approximately 3.519, including the line, but does not identify the optimal ratio.

     References:
     A. D. Procaccia and M. Tennenholtz, Approximate Mechanism Design without Money, EC 2009: https://doi.org/10.1145/1566374.1566401
     H. Chan, J. Lin and C. Wang, Randomized Strategyproof Facility Location: Two Facilities and Beyond, 2026: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22484
description: What is the smallest worst-case expected social-cost approximation ratio achievable by a truthful-in-expectation mechanism placing two facilities on the real line without payments? Agents privately report their locations, each incurs distance to the nearer facility, and social cost is the sum of these distances.

source_id: Game theory, social choice and fair division/15A
area: Game theory, social choice and fair division
author: Noam Nisan
title: Constant-factor truthful subadditive combinatorial auctions
text:
Can a randomized dominant-strategy truthful mechanism obtain a constant fraction of optimal welfare for arbitrary subadditive bidders using polynomially many demand queries and polynomial computation? Values are worst-case inputs, rather than draws from a known prior, and truthfulness in expectation is allowed.

     Remark: The demand-query model is essential; value-query lower bounds and prior-dependent prophet mechanisms do not settle this question.

     References:
     S. Dobzinski, N. Nisan and M. Schapira, Truthful Randomized Mechanisms for Combinatorial Auctions, JCSS 2012: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcss.2011.02.010
     S. Assadi, T. Kesselheim and S. Singla, Improved Truthful Mechanisms for Subadditive Combinatorial Auctions: Breaking the Logarithmic Barrier, SODA 2021: https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01420
description: Can a randomized dominant-strategy truthful mechanism obtain a constant fraction of optimal welfare for arbitrary subadditive bidders using polynomially many demand queries and polynomial computation? Values are worst-case inputs, rather than draws from a known prior, and truthfulness in expectation is allowed.

source_id: Game theory, social choice and fair division/17A
area: Game theory, social choice and fair division
author: Éva Tardos
title: Constant price of stability for undirected network design
text:
In an undirected graph, each player chooses a path between its own terminal pair and each used edge’s cost is split equally among its users. Must there always be a pure Nash equilibrium whose total purchased-edge cost is at most a universal constant times the minimum feasible network cost?

     Remark: The question allows arbitrary terminal pairs; constant bounds for broadcast or other single-source special cases do not settle it.

     References:
     E. Anshelevich, A. Dasgupta, J. Kleinberg, É. Tardos, T. Wexler and T. Roughgarden, The Price of Stability for Network Design with Fair Cost Allocation, 2008: https://doi.org/10.1137/070680096
description: In an undirected graph, each player chooses a path between its own terminal pair and each used edge’s cost is split equally among its users. Must there always be a pure Nash equilibrium whose total purchased-edge cost is at most a universal constant times the minimum feasible network cost?

source_id: Game theory, social choice and fair division/18A
area: Game theory, social choice and fair division
author: David M. Pennock
title: The sharp selfishness threshold for manipulation-resistant tournaments
text:
Does every number of teams admit a monotone, Condorcet-consistent randomized tournament rule satisfying 2-NM₁? Under this condition a pair cannot gain more total winning probability by fixing its match than the probability sacrificed by the team that loses deliberately.

     Remark: The December 2025 construction already achieves the constant threshold 11; the open conjecture is the optimal threshold 1, not merely the existence of any constant.

     References:
     D. Pennock, A. Schvartzman and E. Xue, Toward Fair and Strategyproof Tournament Rules for Tournaments with Partially Transferable Utilities, 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.10346
     D. Pennock, D. Schoepflin and K. Wang, Strategyproof Tournament Rules for Teams with a Constant Degree of Selfishness, December 2025, Section 6: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05235
description: Does every number of teams admit a monotone, Condorcet-consistent randomized tournament rule satisfying 2-NM₁? Under this condition a pair cannot gain more total winning probability by fixing its match than the probability sacrificed by the team that loses deliberately.

source_id: Game theory, social choice and fair division/20A
area: Game theory, social choice and fair division
author: Brendan Lucier
title: Black-box conversion to dominant-strategy truthfulness without expected-welfare loss
text:
Can a polynomial-query black-box transformation turn any allocation algorithm for independent, known single-parameter value distributions into a truthful-in-expectation dominant-strategy mechanism preserving its expected welfare? The transformation learns feasibility only from the allocation algorithm’s outputs; the benchmark is average welfare under the prior, not a worst-case approximation guarantee.

     Remark: Bayesian incentive-compatible reductions are known, and stronger MIDR reductions or preservation of worst-case approximation are impossible; neither answers this expected-welfare DSIC question.

     References:
     E. Gergatsouli, B. Lucier and C. Tzamos, The Complexity of Black-Box Mechanism Design with Priors, 2019: https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.10794
     B. Lucier, Black-Box Reductions to DSIC Mechanism Design, contributed open problem, 2026: https://github.com/aieconcs/econcs-bench/blob/main/black-box-dsic-mechanism-design/PROBLEM.md
description: Can a polynomial-query black-box transformation turn any allocation algorithm for independent, known single-parameter value distributions into a truthful-in-expectation dominant-strategy mechanism preserving its expected welfare? The transformation learns feasibility only from the allocation algorithm’s outputs; the benchmark is average welfare under the prior, not a worst-case approximation guarantee.

source_id: Game theory, social choice and fair division/21A
area: Game theory, social choice and fair division
author: Itai Ashlagi
title: The optimal truthful approximation for multi-hospital kidney exchange
text:
What is the best worst-case approximation ratio attainable by a randomized mechanism truthful in expectation for two-way kidney exchange with arbitrarily many hospitals? Hospitals own vertex sets, maximize their own matched patients, and may hide vertices and match them internally with their remaining unmatched vertices.

     Remark: The paper gives factor 2 and a randomized impossibility bound of 8/7; the deterministic factor-2 lower bound does not settle the randomized question. The target concerns two-cycles and unrestricted hospital counts, not the better-understood two-hospital case.

     References:
     I. Ashlagi, F. Fischer, I. A. Kash and A. D. Procaccia, Mix and Match: A Strategyproof Mechanism for Multi-Hospital Kidney Exchange, 2015: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089982561300081X
description: What is the best worst-case approximation ratio attainable by a randomized mechanism truthful in expectation for two-way kidney exchange with arbitrarily many hospitals? Hospitals own vertex sets, maximize their own matched patients, and may hide vertices and match them internally with their remaining unmatched vertices.
